Motorola has kicked off its Android 17 rollout for the Razr Fold, marking the first major patch for the company’s first book-style foldable, and the start of a potentially interest 7 years of software support.

The Motorola Razr Fold launched with Android 16 back in May 2026, and it remains a really good option for those looking to pick up a book-style foldable in the US. On top of solid specs across the board, it also carries the promise of 7 years of software support, something that few other Moto devices can tout.

Sources indicate that but nowhere was it promises that Motorola would speed things up at all. A little over 3 months after Motorola confirmed the upgrade and several weeks after other Motorola devices were updated to Android 17, the Motorola Razr Fold is finally getting its own Android 17 update.

It has been revealed that rolling out now, Android 17 for the Razr Fold is a 4.15GB~ update that appears to be available at least somewhat broadly. Reports are popping up on Reddit including one report from the EU (Hungary, specifically), with another user apparently in a Spanish-speaking region also seeing the update.

According to recent reports, we’re still waiting to see if the upgrade is available in the US (there’s a backlog of updates on our unit), but it’s certainly an update to look forward to. Apparently, Motorola finally fixed a weird UI glitch that affected the Telegram app, something we ran into when using the device earlier this year.

It’s great to see the update out, but it’s noteworthy that Motorola is not setting a particularly encouraging precedent here. Razr Fold is one of the firm’s first devices to be promised 7 years of OS updates and software support, and its flagship-tier status certainly would have most expecting it to be updated ahead of some of Motorola’s more affordable, lower-tier devices that were updated over a month ago. Whatever the case, hopefully Motorola will speed things up over the next few years, especially with its $1,600 flagship Signature 27 on the horizon with the same software promises.

A Space Probe Returns to Asteroids Where NASA Tested Planetary Defense Systems

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1031 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s mostly been the subject of Hollywood movies, but one day, an asteroid or comet could collide with Earth and cause serious damage.
  • Astronomers predict that in mid-April 2029, the asteroid Apophis will fly by Earth.
  • According to recent reports, in the past few decades, there’s been enormous progress in making these kinds of predictions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s mostly been the subject of Hollywood movies, but one day, an asteroid or comet could collide with Earth and cause serious damage. We don't have to look all that far back for an example. In 1908, in an incident now known as the “Tunguska Event,” a space rock, likely a few dozen meters wide, exploded over Siberia. Though scientists weren’t able to visit the site for another two decades, the landscape was still scarred from the explosion.

Astronomers predict that in mid-April 2029, the asteroid Apophis will fly by Earth. The 450-meter-wide body will miss us at a distance of only 19,000 miles. That’s about 12 times closer to us than the moon and much closer than many satellites. It will even be visible to the naked eye.

According to recent reports, in the past few decades, there’s been enormous progress in making these kinds of predictions. As space probes deepen our knowledge of small bodies in the solar system, astronomers have increasingly reliable and detailed data for finding potentially hazardous asteroids. Our ability to respond to such a threat, however, is another story. This is the missing and extremely important link—planetary defense technology that could allow us to deflect a dangerous object in time.

It has been revealed that in a sci-fi flick, such situations are often solved with a nuclear bomb. But in the real world, blowing up a big space rock into tiny bits is not ideal. Instead, it’s better to alter the asteroid's orbit. Everything in the vacuum of space is in motion. Our own planet travels about 20 miles every second. If the object hurtling towards us can be slowed down and thus reach the meeting point a little later, it will simply miss the Earth.

Four years ago, this was essentially what NASA tested on a pair of celestial bodies known as Didymos and Dimorphos. Astronomers at the Kitt Peak Observatory discovered Didymos, an asteroid measuring 780 meters across, 30 years ago. A few years later, Czech astronomer Petr Pravec observed that this asteroid had a “moonlet” orbiting it about every 12 hours. This smaller body, measuring about 151 meters in diameter, was then named Dimorphos.

The paired objects were a perfect testing ground for the kind of deflection a planetary defense system would involve. Locked in on these targets, NASA launched the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) in late 2021. Nearly a year later, the DART probe crashed into Dimorphos.

Scientists had hoped that the impact of the probe—which was barreling toward the asteroids at over 13,000 miles per hour—could shorten the period of the mini-moon's orbit by a minute or more. In the end, it was slowed down by 33 minutes. This major deviation was caused by the ejection of debris, leading to a much greater recoil than what was produced by the impact itself. In addition, the orbital speed of both asteroids around the sun also slowed. And in a sense, Dimorphos briefly became a comet—the debris released by the impact creating a long tail behind it.

It has been revealed that but questions remain about the longer-term impacts of this test. In October 2024, the European Space Agency (ESA) sent off the space probe Hera to rendezvous with both asteroids. After a flyby of Mars, the probe began its arrival phase this past October. It took its first image about 800 miles away, and the first detailed image of Didymos was published in early November.

Now in their vicinity, Hera will study both bodies in depth. Though there’s much we can learn about asteroids by observing them from our planet, nothing can replace close-up exploration, and this will be the first time a binary asteroid system will be explored in detail. One of the mission's goals is to find out how such asteroid pairs form. Didymos is also interesting for its rapid rotation, turning once every 2.3 hours—placing it on the very edge of stability.

But of course, beyond this traditional astronomy research, which could also take place at another set of binary asteroids, Hera will investigate the consequences of the DART mission. This will include studying the impact site. Because there are so many knowns about the impact itself, scientists can also use this opportunity to understand craters more broadly, answering questions such as whether the strength of the material or gravity plays a more decisive role in crater formation.

It has been revealed that hera will also determine the exact mass of Dimorphos, an vital detail in assessing the effectiveness of the DART mission as a test of planetary defense technology. The probe also contains a lidar instrument for mapping the asteroid's topography and instruments for investigating the chemical composition of the surface. Additionally, we can expect to see detailed images of the asteroids taken with a resolution of 1 meter per pixel.

In a recent development, the probe is also carrying two miniature, cube-shaped satellites, called “CubeSats” for short, which it will deploy in January 2027. In Earth’s orbit, CubeSats are often used for simple experiments, including student projects, and they can even be stacked together to create larger satellites.

Hera’s CubeSats, named Juventas and Milani, will attempt to land on the surface. Using radar capable of probing up to a depth of 100 meters, Juventas will focus on geophysical exploration of the asteroid Dimorphos. Additionally, a gravimeter on board will measure how the gravity on Dimorphos changes during its orbit due to the parent asteroid, Didymos. Meanwhile, Milani will carry out a detailed investigation of the asteroids’ surface composition and will search for traces of dust and the volatile substances contained within many space rocks.

According to current intends, this main phase of the Hera probe's mission is expected to last until the summer of next year, and findings from this probe will likely only become more relevant, not just as Apophis approaches, but even after it slings back into space. In the year 2000, we knew of only 300 near-Earth asteroids—those that approach Earth or directly cross its orbit. Today, we know of over 43,000.

Why Sony's fresh digital Walkmans cost thousands of dollars

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The numbers on Sony’s latest Walkmans raise some questions that the spec sheets don’t answer.
  • According to recent reports, some of us have never owned a Walkman, and judging by the sticker prices of the latest models, that may never change.
  • The implied explanation for those insane prices is the premium components and materials Sony uses across the models.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The numbers on Sony’s latest Walkmans raise some questions that the spec sheets don’t answer.

According to recent reports, some of us have never owned a Walkman, and judging by the sticker prices of the latest models, that may never change. Sony never stopped making them, though, and on October 15 the firm opened pre-orders for three new models. The cheapest, the NW-ZX900, costs a staggering $1,899. The NW-WM1AM3 sits above it at $2,999, while the gold-plated NW-WM1ZM3 flagship will set you back almost six grand.

The implied explanation for those insane prices is the premium components and materials Sony uses across the models. And while those parts aren't cheap, they don't explain why both less-expensive models cost more than twice what their predecessors did. They also don't explain why the $5,899 flagship offers no significant improvement on paper over the NW-ZX900, with essentially the same output from the headphone amp and a shorter battery life, at up to 33 hours of hi-res playback. Nor do they explain why that flagship works out to about $3,800 in Japan once sales tax is taken out. It's clear Sony is selling these as luxury goods to a small audiophile market, but as with a lot of audiophile gear, the returns shrink fast as the price goes up.

In a recent development, the $5,899 WM1ZM3 flagship's main chassis is machined from 99.99 percent pure oxygen-free copper and then gold-plated. The previous flagship's aluminum rear panel gets swapped for a copper one, and even the screws get a low-resistance gold plating, which Sony claims gives a more stable ground connection and, in turn, stronger bass and a wider soundstage. Inside, there's thick Kimber Kable wiring borrowed from Sony's DMP-Z1 desktop player, a second large polymer capacitor and a copper block over the digital circuitry that's 34 percent heavier than before. All that metal weighs a hefty 670g (around 1.5 pounds), up from the 2022 model's 490g (around 1.1 pounds).

According to recent reports, the more modest $1,899 ZX900, meanwhile, has a machined aluminum chassis with a gold-plated copper rear panel, just like the $2,999 WM1AM3, and the same ultra-low-noise voltage regulator and crystal oscillators as its pricier siblings. All three use Sony's S-Master HX digital amp and are rated at 250mW per channel from the 4.4mm balanced jack, while storage goes from 64GB to 128GB to 256GB. So for the extra $4,000 between the ZX900 and the flagship, you're getting copper, better wiring, capacitors and more storage.

In its review of the $3,699 WM1ZM2, What Hi-Fi? pointed out that the (much) cheaper WM1AM2 shared most of the flagship's specs and engineering, and docked the ZM2 points for its limited power output. That's not addressed by the ZM3, either, since it's rated for the same 250mW per channel. AV Watch heard more of a step-up in transparency and space from the ZM2, but still called the AM2 excellent value for money. If an extra $2,300 paid for a difference that reviews couldn't agree on back in 2022, it's difficult to see how one could justify the $4,000 gap between the ZX900 and the ZM3 today.

Industry observers note that the NW-WM1Z, Sony's gold-plated Walkman from 2016, debuted at $3,199. In 2022, the WM1ZM2 became Sony's $3,699 Walkman for over-the-top audiophiles alongside a $1,399 WM1AM2. The ZX707 followed in 2023 at $899. This year, the WM1ZM3's price has jumped 59 percent, but both cheaper models have also more than doubled in price, meaning there's no longer a premium Walkman option under $1,000. Astell&Kern's Android-based SP4000 flagship, meanwhile, lists at $4,290, or about $1,600 less than the ZM3.

Retailers in Japan expect the WM1ZM3 to sell for around ¥655,000 and the ZX900 for around ¥215,000. Take out the 10 percent consumption tax that's included in Japanese shelf prices and convert at September's average of about ¥156 to the dollar, and that's roughly $3,800 and $1,250. In other words, US buyers are paying more than 50 percent more for the same players. Copper hit a record of around $14,850 a metric ton in August, but even a 670g (around 1.5 pounds) Walkman made entirely of copper would only contain about $10 worth of it.

Industry observers note that so if you're not already someone who will happily spend thousands on headphones and amps, the Walkman for you is still the NW-A306, which debuted at $349 in 2023 and is still on sale. The newly introduced trio replaces Sony's high-end players, not that one, and if you're set on one of them, the ZX900 gets you most of the flagship's hardware for the money. In essence, Sony has built all three Walkmans from expensive parts. But the jump in price since the previous generation looks like it has more to do with what die-hard audiophiles will pay for one, rather than what they cost to build.
